Naveen: why did you wave me off in the canteen yesterday
Naveen: like a fly 😅
Farhan: wait what
Naveen: you did this with your hand, palm out, shoo shoo
Farhan: OH. I was carrying a full tray of hot rasam and you were right behind me
Farhan: I meant 'give me a bit of space', not 'go away'
Naveen: I thought you were fed up with me
Farhan: no no. I should've said 'one sec, hot tray!'
Naveen: yes please, use words
Farhan: deal. the hand is for trays, not for you
Naveen: 😄 ok. lunch tomorrow?
Farhan: yes. I'll carry the rasam, you hold the door

qa.q: What was Farhan carrying when the hand went out?
qa.a: Farhan was carrying a full tray of hot rasam.

qa.q: What did Naveen think Farhan's wave meant, and how did Naveen feel about it?
qa.a: Naveen thought Farhan was fed up and felt brushed aside and worried about the friendship. Farhan had only wanted space because of the hot tray.

qa.q: What could Farhan say next time instead of waving?
qa.a: Farhan can say, "one sec, hot tray!" A few words show whether the wave means not now, give me air, or stay away.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt on learning how the wave had been read?
qa.a: Farhan probably felt surprised and a little sorry, replying 'wait what' and then admitting it would have been better to say 'one sec, hot tray!'

grounding: A teenager's move-back hand wave is read as rejection but only meant space, and words clarify.

passage: At the crowded bus door in Pipli, Wasim pushed his palm out toward Suraj. "Back, back." Suraj stepped away, stung. Two aunties nearby waved their hands even harder at the people behind them, and nobody seemed offended. On the bus, Wasim saw Suraj sitting stiffly. "You okay?" "You waved me off like I was a stray goat." Wasim winced. "Sorry. My arm was squashed and I couldn't breathe. I only wanted a little air, not for you to go away." Suraj's shoulders eased. "Then just say 'thoda peeche'." Wasim laughed. "Thoda peeche, yaar. Done."

qa.q: In which place did Wasim push his palm out?
qa.a: At the crowded bus door in Pipli.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when Wasim waved Suraj back, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Suraj felt stung and possibly insulted, and sat stiffly on the bus. Suraj also compared it to being waved off like a stray goat.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time he needs space?
qa.a: He can add words like 'thoda peeche' with the wave. A verbal follow-up clarifies without shaming anyone.

qa.q: Why might the aunties react differently to the same wave?
qa.a: People differ on how blunt a hand wave is, and in a crowd it is common. The aunties may see it as normal, while Suraj took it personally.

grounding: A teenager's move-back gesture can mean give me air rather than stay away, and words clarify.

passage:
At the end of the 800-metre race in Cape Town, Zanele crossed the line second and bent over, hands on her knees, gasping. Her teammates swarmed her, shouting, patting her back. Marek pushed in closest, waving his phone. "Look, I filmed the whole thing!"
Zanele flapped a hand at him without looking up, a quick push-away wave.
Marek stepped back, his smile slipping. He lowered the phone and turned to go.
Zanele saw his face. She straightened, still panting. "Marek, wait. That wasn't 'go away.' That was 'I can't breathe yet.'"
He laughed, relieved. "Sorry. I crowded you."
"Just give me one minute of air. Then I want to see the video."
A minute later, they watched it together on the bench.

qa.q: What did Marek film?
qa.a: The whole race.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling when Zanele waved him back?
qa.a: Marek felt hurt and rejected, thinking the wave meant she didn't want him there.

qa.q: What did Zanele do that cleared things up without shaming Marek?
qa.a: She quickly added words to explain the wave meant she needed air, not that he should leave, and invited him back a minute later.

qa.q: How did Zanele experience the crowding after the race?
qa.a: Zanele felt overwhelmed and breathless, needing space to recover before she could enjoy the attention.

grounding: After a race, a teenager's push-away wave is read as rejection until she adds words to explain she only needed air.

passage:
In the corridor outside the exam hall, Bhupen hurried up to Sharmila as soon as she came out. "What did you get for question four? Was it forty-two? I got thirty-eight, did you—"
Sharmila held up a hand, palm out, and moved it slightly toward him, meaning back up.
Bhupen stopped mid-sentence and took a step back, frowning. "Okay, fine."
Sharmila took a breath. "Sorry, Bhupen. It's not you. I just can't talk about answers right after. It makes my head spin. Give me ten minutes?"
Bhupen's frown softened. "Oh. My sister's the same."
Sharmila nodded. After ten minutes and a cold drink from the canteen, she found him. "Forty-two," she said. "I think."

qa.q: What answer did Bhupen say he got for question four?
qa.a: Thirty-eight.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she held up her hand?
qa.a: Sharmila felt overwhelmed and stressed, needing a break from talking about exam answers right after the test.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that kept things respectful?
qa.a: She added words to explain it wasn't about Bhupen and asked for ten minutes, instead of leaving the wave to speak for itself.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen the hand gesture at first?
qa.a: Bhupen probably felt pushed away and a little offended, thinking Sharmila didn't want to talk to him at all.

grounding: Outside an exam hall, a teenager's move-back gesture could mean go away or not now, and a verbal follow-up clarifies it.

passage:
Hi Arnab,
I'm sorry about the wedding. When the baraat reached the gate and everyone was pushing, you came up behind me and put your arm around my shoulder to pull me into the dancing. I shoved your arm off and waved you away, hard, without saying a word.
I saw your face. You thought I was angry with you.
I wasn't. The crowd was so thick I felt like I couldn't breathe, and the dhol was so loud my chest was shaking. I needed air, not a fight.
I should have said, "Give me a minute, I'm squashed," instead of just waving you off.
Next family function, let's find a corner first and then dance.
Vikas

qa.q: What was so loud at the wedding that Vikas's chest was shaking?
qa.a: The dhol.

qa.q: What was Arnab likely feeling when Vikas waved Arnab away?
qa.a: Arnab likely felt hurt and confused, reading the wave as anger when Arnab only wanted to include Vikas.

qa.q: What would have worked better than just waving Arnab off?
qa.a: Saying a few words like "Give me a minute, I'm squashed" would have made the meaning clear without hurting Arnab.

qa.q: If you were Arnab, how might this letter feel?
qa.a: You might feel relieved and understood, knowing the shove was about the crowd and not about you.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager explains that a push-away wave in a crowded baraat meant needing air, not anger, and wishes words had come with it.

passage: So, Jomon, you asked on the way home why I waved you off at the canteen counter. This is Chinmay, owning up. That hand thing, the quick flick like shoo, I did it because the queue was crushing me and you were right at my shoulder, and I felt I couldn't breathe. It meant give me air. Not go away. But I saw your face drop, and you went and sat with Anoop without a word. At home my Ammamma does that same flick at the vegetable seller to mean not now, and nobody minds. In your house I think it's rude, right? So I should have said it in words, something like, "Sorry, I'm a bit squashed, give me a second?" I'm saying it now, late. Save me a seat tomorrow?

qa.q: Where did Chinmay wave Jomon off?
qa.a: At the canteen counter.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling in the queue?
qa.a: Chinmay felt crushed and breathless and needed air, not annoyed with Jomon.

qa.q: What could Chinmay have said with the wave to avoid shaming Jomon?
qa.a: A few words like 'Sorry, I'm a bit squashed, give me a second?' to show it meant space, not rejection.

qa.q: How did Jomon seem to take the wave?
qa.a: Jomon's face dropped and Jomon went to sit with Anoop without a word, likely feeling hurt and brushed off.

grounding: It illustrates a hand wave meaning give me air being read as go away, with family habits differing on bluntness and words clarifying it.
